opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't an obvious decision at first. When I started, I wasn't sure whether a PhD was the best use of those years. There's always the question: should I go to industry, start something, or keep doing research? But over time I realized MIT gave me something that's very hard to find elsewhere, which is the freedom to work on problems that might not have an immediate payoff but could matter a lot in the long run.

For me, that problem was making high-performance computer graphics and physical simulation much easier to program. In industry, it's hard to justify spending years building a new programming language and compiler, which eventually became Taichi, because the return isn't clear at the beginning. In a PhD, you can take that risk. You can say, "I think this is the right direction," and then spend time going deep on it.

The people mattered a lot too. At MIT you're surrounded by advisors and peers who are extremely strong and who push you to think more rigorously. You get feedback that makes your ideas sharper. And there's a culture of building real things, not just writing papers, which fit my personality really well.

So eventually I saw the PhD not as "delaying real life" but as an investment. It let me build skills, a body of work, and a community around open-source tools. Later, when we started a company, a lot of that foundation came directly from those years. Looking back, I think it was definitely worthwhile.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't obvious to me at first. When I got to MIT, I had the feeling a lot of people have — that a PhD is a long time, and the industry was moving so fast that I worried I'd be missing out. I'd already done a bunch of systems work during my undergrad at Tsinghua, and I could have gone and worked at a big company right away.

But a few things changed my mind. The first was working with Fredo Durand and Bill Freeman. They gave me an enormous amount of freedom. I could spend months on something that didn't obviously "pay off," and nobody was asking for a quarterly deliverable. That's very rare. In industry, you usually need to justify what you're doing within a short time horizon. At MIT I could ask a question like, "why is it so painful to write high-performance physics simulation code?" and actually sit with it for a year or two.

That's basically where Taichi came from. If I'd been at a company, I think I would have just written another CUDA kernel and moved on, because that's what the deadline would have demanded. Being in a research environment let me step back and build a compiler and a language instead of a one-off solution. That turned out to matter much more in the long run.

The second thing was the people. The density of talent at MIT is just unusual. My officemates, the people down the hall — you'd have a random conversation at lunch and it would turn into a paper, or at least a much better understanding of some problem. I learned a lot of graphics, a lot of compilers, a lot of machine learning, just by being around people who were much better than me at those things.

And third, honestly, I came to see the PhD as training in how to think, not just a credential. You learn how to pick a problem, how to tell when an idea is actually good versus just sounds good, how to write and communicate so that other people can build on your work. Those skills ended up being more useful to me when I started a company than any specific technical knowledge.

So I'd say I didn't walk in thinking "this is clearly worth it." I kind of grew into that view. By the end, I felt the five years gave me something I couldn't have gotten anywhere else — the time and space to build something ambitious, and the people to build it with.
